scope: Missing New York 8+ grand-jury resisters and Arthur Majid Barnes discovered during December12th Movement research; distinguish their actual affiliations.

dttk.label: Death to the Klan, June 1985, scan page8 / printed p.9: individual grand-jury confinement dates; page image reviewed. Page3 joint prisoner statement independently names the eight resisters.

militant.label: The Militant, July 26, 1985, pp.7,13: eight resisters held at Metropolitan Correctional Center, five still imprisoned; Wanda Wareham released June18. Extracted article reviewed.

cocilovo.label: Matter of Cocilovo, 618 F. Supp.1378 (S.D.N.Y.1985): retrospective list of named contemnors, release dates and approximate custody lengths, footnote1.

ford.label: Matter of Ford, 615 F. Supp.259 (S.D.N.Y.July26,1985): individual start date, institution, political activity and release decision.

thomas.label: Matter of Thomas, 614 F. Supp.983 (S.D.N.Y.July26,1985): individual start date, medical studies, political activity and release decision.

parish.label: Matter of Parish, 613 F. Supp.356 (S.D.N.Y.July24,1985), addendum July25: release decision and political-solidarity reasoning.

d12m.label: December12th Movement, October17,2024, New York8+ anniversary: Dorrie Clay and Wanda Wareham named as grand-jury resisters, separately from defendants.

acoli.label: Sundiata Acoli, A Brief History of the New Afrikan Prison Struggle, p.13: Arthur Majeed Barnes, Abdul Haqq Muhammad and Robert Taylor arrested July16,1987 and later imprisoned for weapon possession.

insurgent.label: The Insurgent, Summer1989, p.22: Arthur Majid Barnes, historical number88-A-7424, listed at Sing Sing. Page image reviewed.

prisoner.name: Lionel Jean-Baptiste
prisoner.description: A New York 8+ grand-jury resister, Lionel Jean-Baptiste spent months in federal custody after refusing to testify in the investigation of Black political activists. Contemporary reporting identifies his November 1984 commitment, and a federal court later recorded his July 1985 release.

cases.charges: Civil contempt — refusal to testify before the grand jury investigating the New York 8+
cases.sentence: Civil confinement for refusing grand-jury testimony; released 1985-07-03. This was coercive civil contempt, not a conviction on the New York 8 defendants' criminal charges.

entries.custody_evidence: Named contemporary confinement report and subsequent individual release evidence establish months of US custody for politically motivated refusal to testify.

case_research.custody_evidence: Individual incarceration and release endpoints supported by the listed sources; the resister is distinct from the criminal defendants.

entries.status_research: Only this completed historical civil-contempt episode is entered. No criminal conviction, maximum eighteen-month term served, DOB/DOD, current custody, or personal support website inferred. Coltrane Chimurenga used the same name as an alias in a separate court caption; contemporary joint statements list Chimurenga and resister Jean-Baptiste separately. Do not identify this witness with Chimurenga, a later Florida denaturalization litigant, or an Illinois judge without independent evidence.

prisoner.name: Michelle Thomas
prisoner.description: Michelle Thomas was a Rutgers medical student and political activist involved with the Sunrise Collective. She was confined at the Metropolitan Correctional Center for refusing to testify before the grand jury investigating the New York 8+. Her incarceration interrupted her medical studies. The court ordered her release after finding that further detention would not make her testify.

prisoner.name: Jean Ford
prisoner.description: Jean Ford was a Harlem Hospital physician and political activist involved in campaigns against apartheid and police brutality. He refused to testify before the grand jury investigating the New York 8+, invoking spousal privilege and political opposition to the investigation. He spent nearly six months at the Metropolitan Correctional Center before the court ordered his release.

prisoner.name: Arthur Majid Barnes
prisoner.description: Arthur Majid Barnes, also named Arthur Majeed Barnes, was a member of the Black Men's Movement Against Crack. Sundiata Acoli identifies him with Abdul Haqq Muhammad and Robert Taylor in a July 1987 upstate New York arrest followed by imprisonment on weapon-possession convictions. A 1989 prisoner-support directory places Barnes at Sing Sing. His exact prison-entry date, term, and later outcome remain unverified.

cases.charges: Weapon possession — individual statutory count not yet verified
cases.sentence: Imprisonment following the July 16, 1987 arrest; listed at Sing Sing in the Summer 1989 Insurgent directory as 88-A-7424. Individual sentence length and release remain unverified.

entries.custody_evidence: Movement history expressly states subsequent imprisonment after the named 1987 arrest; the 1989 directory independently identifies Barnes as a prisoner at Sing Sing, confirming custody beyond initial arrest.

case_research.custody_evidence: Subsequent prison custody is expressly reported and corroborated by an institutional prisoner listing; the arrest day is not treated as the date of prison entry.

entries.status_research: Historical custody verified. Neither current imprisonment nor release is asserted; both flags false and narrative explicitly leaves later outcome unknown. The 1989 listing is not an incarceration-start date, and the historical number is kept in case prose rather than a current inmate-number field. No demographic or vital data inferred.
